 An address appears in `codes_changed` when its code hash at the time of the `TXTRACE` call differs from its code hash at transaction start. As with `EXTCODEHASH`, the code hash is computed over the code as stored: an [EIP-7702](./eip-7702.md) delegation indicator is hashed itself and is not followed to the code it delegates to. An account that does not exist counts as having the empty-code hash, where `EXTCODEHASH` would return `0`. The table therefore includes contracts created by the transaction, whose `codehash_before` is the empty-code hash, and delegation indicators the transaction installed, changed, or cleared. An account that a `CREATE`/`CREATE2` leaves with empty code is not enumerated, as it has no code change.
 
-An address appears in `nonces_changed` when its nonce at the time of the `TXTRACE` call differs from its nonce at transaction start. An account that does not exist counts as having nonce `0`. The table includes `tx.sender` whenever `APPROVE` increments its account nonce in the validation prefix, and also includes any account that executed `CREATE` or `CREATE2` and any contract the transaction created.
+An address appears in `nonces_changed` when its nonce at the time of the `TXTRACE` call differs from its nonce at transaction start. An account that does not exist counts as having nonce `0`. The table includes `tx.sender` whenever `APPROVE` increments its account nonce in the validation prefix, and also includes any account that executed `CREATE` or `CREATE2` and any contract the transaction created. If a transaction's replay protection is kept in contract storage instead of the account nonce, `APPROVE` writes that storage, and the write appears in `slots_changed` rather than in `nonces_changed`.
 
 An account that [EIP-6780](./eip-6780.md) deletes at the end of the transaction appears as the execution body left it, since the deletion happens after the last frame. A contract created and destroyed in the same transaction therefore still appears in `codes_changed` and `nonces_changed`.

index 81d0372e..d7b8181c 100644
--- a/EIPS/eip-8151.md
+++ b/EIPS/eip-8151.md
@@ -17,7 +17,7 @@ This EIP modifies the `ecRecover` precompile at address `0x000000000000000000000
 
 ## Motivation
 
-EOAs can use [EIP-7702](./eip-7702.md) as a bridge to post-quantum authorization. After migration, the account's non-empty code no longer matches the EIP-7702 delegation format `0xef0100 || delegate_address`, so [EIP-3607](./eip-3607.md) disables its ECDSA transaction authority at the protocol level. However, `ecRecover` ignores account state. A quantum-capable attacker deriving the old ECDSA private key could still authorize token transfers through contracts, including [ERC-20](./eip-20.md) `permit` implementations ([ERC-2612](./eip-2612.md)). This EIP applies the same rule to `ecRecover`: recovery returns empty output when the account has non-empty raw code that is not a valid EIP-7702 delegation indicator. As a result, after the account has migrated to post-quantum authorization, the old ECDSA private key can no longer be used for contract authorization that relies on `ecRecover`.
+EOAs can use [EIP-7702](./eip-7702.md) as a bridge to post-quantum authorization. After migration, the account has regular deployed code instead of an EIP-7702 delegation indicator `0xef0100 || delegate_address`, so [EIP-3607](./eip-3607.md) disables protocol-level ECDSA transaction origination. However, `ecRecover` ignores account state. A quantum-capable attacker deriving the old ECDSA private key could still authorize token transfers through contracts, including [ERC-20](./eip-20.md) `permit` implementations ([ERC-2612](./eip-2612.md)). This EIP applies the same rule to `ecRecover`: recovery returns empty output when the account has non-empty raw code that is not a valid EIP-7702 delegation indicator. As a result, after the account has migrated to post-quantum authorization, the old ECDSA private key can no longer be used for contract authorization that relies on `ecRecover`.
